headline: Approved amendments to proposed zoning for small roof-mounted wind energy systems, and recommended the ordinance for a joint public hearing.
summary: The committee discussed allowing small roof-mounted wind energy systems as a permitted use, similar to rooftop solar. Members lowered the capacity limit from 15 kilowatts to 10 kilowatts and raised the height limit from 10 feet to 20 feet. The committee then sent the amended ordinance forward with a positive recommendation for a joint public hearing with the Planning Board and City Council.
decisions: Approved amendments to the proposed zoning ordinance for roof-mounted wind energy systems, by roll call vote 3-0.
Recommended the amended ordinance for a joint public hearing with the Planning Board and City Council, by roll call vote 3-0.

City of Salem, Massachusetts 
 
“Know Your Rights Under the Open Meeting Law, M.G.L. c. 30A ss. 18-25 and  
City Ordinance Sections 2-2028 through 2-2033.” 
 
The City Council Committee on     Ordinances, Licenses and Legal Affairs co-posted Committee of the 
Whole______________________________________________________________________________  
met in the Council Chamber on _August 17, 2026__________ at ______6:00______P.M. 
for the purpose of discussing the matters(s) listed below.  Notice of this meeting was posted on  
___  July 29, 2026__ at ___        10:20 A.M._________________ 
(This meeting is being recorded) 
ATTENDANCE 
OLLA – Varela (chair), Holappa (zoom), King (temporary appointment to committee for this meeting only).   COW – Merkl and 
Davis. 
ABSENT WERE:  OLLA –  Hapworth, Prosniewski,  Smith.  COW - Flynn, Sydoriak and Turowski 
#386 Ordinance Relative to Zoning – Roof-Mounted Wind Energy Systems 
Varela – Appointed King to OLLA committee for this meeting only.  He supports allowing roof-mounted wind energy systems in 
Salem, arguing that residents should be empowered to improve their own energy resiliency. He noted that wind complements 
solar because wind tends to be stronger at night and during the winter, while solar is most effective during longer summer 
days. 
His main concern is that current zoning regulations create a barrier to residents adopting small-scale wind energy systems. He 
stated that, since Salem already permits residential solar installations, the city should similarly make it legal and practical for 
residents to install roof-mounted wind systems. 
King – She explained that the proposed ordinance would update Salem’s zoning code to allow small roof-mounted wind energy 
systems by right on all buildings, with size restrictions to ensure they remain small-scale residential systems. She emphasized 
using the term “wind energy systems” rather than “windmills” because commercially available systems come in a variety of 
designs, including units that resemble small fans. The proposed ordinance change is intended to treat rooftop wind similarly to 
residential solar while giving residents another option for producing or offsetting energy. 
She stated that rooftop wind can be a useful alternative or complement to solar, particularly because wind and solar can 
produce energy at different times of day and year. Solar incentives have declined, and not every home has a roof that is well 
suited for solar because of its orientation or location. Small wind systems could therefore provide another way for 
homeowners to reduce energy use, particularly in a coastal, windy community like Salem. She also noted that these systems 
are much more common in European countries, where stronger energy and building-code incentives encourage their use. 
The ordinance establishes clear limits to keep the systems small at no more than 15 kilowatts of capacity per turbine and no 
more than 10 feet in height. These limits are based on the size of small systems currently available on the market and are 
intended to let Salem gain experience with the technology without opening the door to larger wind installations. She 
characterized this as a way for Salem, as a coastal community with climate-resilience goals, to “dip our toes in the water.”
The zoning changes would add roof-mounted wind energy systems as a permitted use by right, similar to rooftop solar. The 
ordinance would also incorporate wind systems into the existing provisions for rooftop solar while establishing the separate 
10-foot height limit. Additional definitions would clarify terms such as wind energy system, capacity, and height. 
Finally, the proposal would clarify the distinction between these small residential rooftop systems and Salem’s existing zoning 
provisions for large-scale industrial/offshore wind development. She said this separation is intended to keep the existing large-
scale wind provisions intact while clearly establishing a separate framework for small rooftop systems. The Assistant City 
Solicitor also reviewed and helped draft the proposed language. 
Discussion –  
The committee discussed a proposed zoning amendment to allow small, roof-mounted wind energy systems as an accessory 
use, largely by aligning them with existing provisions for rooftop solar. Councillors focused first on basic technical parameters, 
particularly the maximum system capacity and overall height. There was broad comfort with reducing the draft capacity limit 
from 15 kilowatts to 10 kilowatts so that wind systems would match the existing 10-kilowatt cap for roof-mounted solar 
installations. Councillors also acknowledged that common rooftop turbines on the market are taller than the 10-foot height 
figure initially contemplated, which pushed the group toward a more realistic upper limit of 20 feet. 
Height and visual impact generated a more detailed conversation. Councillors noted that residents are generally most 
concerned with how far equipment projects above the existing roofline, rather than the absolute height of the structure. 
Under current zoning, certain elements such as spires, chimneys, antennas, and the proposed roof-mounted wind systems are 
exempt from strict building height limits. This raised the concern that a house already close to the maximum height could still 
install a tall turbine at the highest point and effectively overshoot what neighbors find reasonable. To address this, councillors 
discussed approaches like capping turbine height at around 20 feet, or tying it to the maximum allowed building height plus an 
additional buffer (for example, 5–10 feet). 
Setbacks were another major point with the committee looking to the existing solar language as a model. Section 4.1.2(8) 
currently requires small and medium ground-mounted solar systems to be at least 10 feet from the front, side, and rear lot 
lines. The simplest proposal was to insert “roof-mounted wind energy systems” into that same clause so the same 10-foot 
setback from property boundaries would apply. Clarification was provided that this is measured from the lot line, not the edge 
of the building: if a structure sits directly on the lot line, a roof turbine must be placed at least 10 feet in from that edge; if the 
house is already well set back, placement on the roof can be more flexible. This approach aims to protect closely spaced 
abutters while allowing more freedom on larger lots. 
The committee also touched on noise, structural load, and governance issues. On noise, informal legal guidance from the 
solicitor suggested that decibel limits are more properly handled under the city’s general noise ordinance rather than in 
zoning, and future experience could drive targeted noise amendments if needed. For structural loading, councillors recognized 
that turbines can weigh significantly more than solar panels and that snow load is a factor, but agreed that these issues are 
best addressed through the building permit process, where applicants must demonstrate that their roofs can safely support 
the systems. At a governance level, several councillors expressed frustration that department heads and the mayor did not 
attend despite invitations, emphasizing that technical staff input is important to defining “reasonable” limits. They discussed 
using two procedural tools to secure that input, sending the proposal to a required joint public hearing with the Planning 
Board, which starts the statutory clock and may spur engagement, or invoking a city charter provision that obligates the mayor 
or a designee to attend and answer written questions submitted a week in advance.  Councillors wanted to proceed cautiously, 
ensuring that expert feedback from the building department and other staff reviews the final technical details before any 
ordinance language is adopted. 
Public Comment –  
Josiah Guthrie spoke in support of modernizing Salem’s zoning regulations to allow small rooftop wind energy systems, stating 
that the city should future-proof its regulations as technology and community needs evolve. The proposed ordinance would 
treat small rooftop wind systems similarly to existing solar regulations. He emphasized that while Salem receives less sunlight 
than the national average, it has an unusually strong wind resource because of its coastal location. He said that Salem currently 
has no meaningful pathway for residents to take advantage of that resource through small-scale wind energy.
Guthrie acknowledged concerns about the economic viability of rooftop wind systems but said that public policy itself is one of 
the major barriers to adoption, alongside the cost of competing energy sources. He said the city should not prevent residents 
from making their own decisions about whether a technology is financially worthwhile. He framed the proposal as part of 
Salem’s broader effort to reduce reliance on fossil fuels, increase energy resilience, and take advantage of local renewable 
resources.  
He also distinguished modern small rooftop systems from the large, traditional wind turbines often associated with noise and 
vibration concerns. He described newer systems as smaller, more adaptable designs, including systems that resemble 
sculptures or flowers, systems with no moving parts, and spiral-based designs intended to work with the wind rather than 
against it. He cited examples from countries such as Germany, Spain, and the Netherlands, where small systems are being used 
to provide a significant portion of household energy needs.  
Finally, Guthrie stated that wind, solar, and battery storage can complement one another, with wind often producing more 
when solar production is lower and batteries storing excess energy for periods when both are less productive. He connected 
the proposal to Salem’s existing climate and resilience commitments, including the Resilient Together partnership with Beverly, 
and urged the Council to expand residents’ renewable-energy options as part of the city’s broader commitment to clean 
energy, resilience, and climate action.  
Vote –  
 
The committee considered and approved a set of amendments to the zoning ordinance to better regulate roof mounted wind 
energy systems.  The discussion emphasized that these changes arose from proactive resident input and collaboration with the 
Ward 5 councillor, and that they are meant to modernize zoning rules while remaining practical for residential use. Councillors 
stressed that many existing ordinances do not reflect current needs or future-facing policy, and that this proposal represents a 
constructive example of community-driven legislative work.  The councillors expressed disappointment that no one from the 
mayor’s office or department heads attended the meeting, although they were invited several weeks in advance.   
 
Under the zoning ordinance for Roof-Mounted Wind Energy Systems, the following amendments were proposed.  The first 
amendment is in Section 3, under definitions.  For the definition of “Wind Energy System, Roof Mounted”, strike 15 kilowatts 
per turbine, and replace it with 10 kilowatts per turbine.   Strike height up to 10 feet and replace it with height up to 20 feet.  
Section 2 will be entirely rewritten so strike the language in subsection 7.  Section 2, Section 4.1.2, subsection 8 - Notes to 
Table of Dimensional Requirements is hereby amended by inserting the line “and roof-mounted wind energy systems” after 
medium-scale ground-mounted solar energy systems.  Also inserting a new subsection 10, which will read “The limitations on 
height of buildings shall apply to roof-mounted wind energy systems, with an additional allowance of 5 feet over the 
maximum height of the building”.  Clarification regarding the setbacks - Section 2 amends Section 4.1.2, which is the Notes to 
Table of Dimensional Requirements, in two ways. The first way is it adds roof-mounted energy systems to subsection 8 that 
has the setback requirements (currently states “Small- and medium-scale ground mounted solar energy systems accessory 
to principal use may be located no closer than ten (10) feet from the front, side, or rear lot line”).  Then the second change 
adds a new subsection 10, which has the height change.  It made more sense to add a new subsection for that, because 
there's no other section in the zoning ordinance that has that type of height with an extra allowance type of language.  Motion 
was made by King and seconded by Holappa for the amendments to proposed ordinance.  Motion carried with roll call vote 3-
0.  King motioned and Holappa seconded to send the amended ordinance with a positive recommendation for a joint public 
hearing with the Planning Board and City Council.  Motion carried with roll call vote 3-0.   
On the motion of C. King the meeting adjourned at 6:52 P.M. 
 
       Andrew Varela                                          mbc 
           (Chairperson)
